content.title: Here are the 2026 Best Picture nominees ranked
content.text: The 98th Academy Awards are just around the corner, bringing renewed debate over which film deserves Hollywood's highest honor: Best Picture.The 2026 nominees for Best Picture are "Bugonia," "F1," "Frankenstein," "Hamnet," "Marty Supreme," "One Battle After Another," "The Secret Agent," "Sentimental Value," "Sinners," and "Train Dreams."Among the most-nominated films for this year's Academy Awards are "Sinners" with 16 nominations, along with "One Battle After Another" with 13 nominations. Following closely behind are "Marty Supreme" and "Frankenstein."After I watched and evaluated each film, here are all of the Best Picture nominees, ranked:10. F1Director: Joseph KosinskiStarring: Brad Pitt, Kerry Condon and Damson Idris Genre: Action/sportsSummary: "F1" follows Sonny Hayes, a Formula 1 driver who returns to the sport from retirement to mentor a rookie prodigy and a struggling team. Where to watch: Apple TVREVIEW: Like many other film lovers, I was quite surprised by the inclusion of "F1" in this year's Best Picture nominees. Now, "F1" is not particularly bad by any means. It does what it is supposed to do – deliver a family-friendly popcorn movie, that is. It's loud, it's clean, and it surely is fast. Plus, the magic that is Hans Zimmer will certainly improve any piece of media. This works very well on a big screen, but I can't imagine any at-home theatre setup would do it justice. Albeit formulaic, "F1" is a blast, and it knows it.9. FrankensteinDirector: Guillermo del ToroStarring: Jacob Elordi, Oscar Isaac, Mia GothGenre: Sci-fi/horrorSummary: This adaptation of the classic Gothic story of Frankenstein depicts a scientist who brings a monstrous creature to life in an experiment.Where to watch: NetflixREVIEW: How many adaptations of "Frankenstein" will we see in our lifetimes? Rather, in Guillermo del Toro's case, does it really matter? His take on the timeless monster tale brings impeccable craftsmanship, filled to the brim with twisted, gnarled imagery and emotional depth that will make you think twice about your empathy toward the unknown, the misunderstood. Oscar Isaac brings his best to what the selfish, wicked character requires. He truly becomes the so-called mad scientist. Jacob Elordi, put frankly, I was not familiar with your game. (Be grateful if this is your introduction to Elordi, as many of us were given the disservice of first seeing him in the 2018 Netflix flop "The Kissing Booth.") "Frankenstein" is an adaptation of one of the most famous stories of all time, a beautiful adaptation, yes. But at what point does it overstay its welcome, and when does the pacing start feeling lethargic? Personally, I find it mostly worth it, but many people won't.8. BugoniaDirector: Yorgos LanthimosStarring: Emma Stone, Jesse Plemons, Aidan DelbisGenre: Sci-fi/comedySummary: Two conspiracy theorists kidnap the CEO of a major company, whom they believe is secretly an alien that plans to destroy Earth. Where to watch: PeacockREVIEW: Both Emma Stone and Jesse Plemons, the stars of "Bugonia," give possibly some of their best performances yet. So much of this film can be summed up as an intense conversation between the two of them, and it works. Only a solid script with magnificent actors can create such long-lasting tension that keeps you sitting straight up, waiting for what's to come. My problem remains with Yorgos Lanthimos in that sometimes, he hasn't quite figured out how to end a story. Without spoiling "Bugonia," it is absurd, stressful and at times disturbing, with an ending so unique that you certainly won't forget it any time soon. But just because it is memorable does not mean it isn't lacking. 7. The Secret AgentDirector: Kleber Mendonça FilhoStarring: Wagner Moura, Udo Kier, Maria Fernanda CândidoGenre: Thriller/crimeSummary: A Brazilian technology specialist fleeing persecution by an authoritarian government hopes to find refuge.Where to watch: HuluREVIEW: While it is labeled a thriller, "The Secret Agent" really is more of a historical drama that transports you straight into 1970s-era Brazil. While it may be shocking to hear this, if you are looking for storytelling that really just relies on vibes, this is the lengthy film for you – and that as a vibe in itself certainly won't click with many different kinds of people. The 161-minute runtime may feel disjointed and slow-moving, but Wagner Moura is worth the watch. 6. Sentimental ValueDirector: Joachim TrierStarring: Renate Reinsve, Stellan Skarsgård, Elle FanningGenre: Drama Summary: After their mother's death, two sisters reunite with their estranged father, a once-famous director who offers one of the sisters a lead role in his new film. Where to watch: RentREVIEW: Every single performance in "Sentimental Value," no matter big or small, feels larger than life. Their interactions feel legitimate, and with such tenderness ingrained within them. When it is watered down to the basics, this is the story of a house, one that breathes and loves and has faced life and death. Yet, on a personal level, I didn't feel emotionally connected to "Sentimental Value" in the way so many others evidently did. The script starts to endure a certain dullness and is underutilized in several key instances, but the many remarkable performances and the brilliance in what they carry make this a wonderfully bittersweet watch. 5. Train DreamsDirector: Clint BentleyStarring: Joel Edgerton, Felicity Jones, William H. MacyGenre: DramaSummary: The story of an American railroad laborer living and working in the early 1900s, Where to watch: NetflixREVIEW: "Train Dreams" is like watching a poem read itself aloud for one man's entire lifetime. It is soft and so deeply caring, it searches for beauty and meaning in the smallest moments. It finds deep value in the individual; it breathes slowly and with intent as the pages turn. It learns eventually that even amid all of the world's pain and suffering, living is worth something. "Train Dreams" also holds one of the greatest scores that cinema has seen in quite some years. It carries such greatness and emotion that it almost feels like we should be unworthy of hearing it. 4. HamnetDirector: Chloé ZhaoStarring: Jessie Buckley, Paul Mescal, Jacobi JupeGenre: DramaSummary: William Shakespeare and his wife cope with loss after the tragic and sudden death of their young son, leading Shakespeare to write his masterpiece "Hamlet."Where to watch: PeacockREVIEW: Noah and Jacobi Jupe, with only mere minutes of screentime each, deliver a pair of performances that should move any person to tears. All one can hope is that both members of this young brother duo win their own Academy Awards one day. Is this the best film of 2025? Unfortunately, no. But the final ten minutes of "Hamnet" contain perhaps one of the greatest sequences of personified grief I have ever witnessed. That, accompanied by Max Richter's "On The Nature of Daylight" playing confidently in the background, creates a powerful explosion of deep sorrow, yet it feels so loving.3. Marty SupremeDirector: Josh SafdieStarring: Timothée Chalamet, Gwyneth Paltrow, Odessa A'zionGenre: Sports dramaSummary: A table tennis prodigy leads a series of high-stakes hustles and schemes to reach a major tournament in Tokyo, Japan. Where to watch: RentREVIEW: If you're looking for a run-of-the-mill sports biopic, turn back now, because this story is everything else. "Marty Supreme" at its true self is a narcissistic pursuit of greatness by any and all means necessary. Never once in 150 minutes does this artistry fall flat or lose its charm; in fact, it simply keeps getting better. What are you willing to do, to sacrifice, to abandon, to reach the top? Just ask Timothée Chalamet's version of Marty Mauser, and I am sure he will scheme an answer. 2. SinnersDirector: Ryan CooglerStarring: Michael B. Jordan, Hailee Steinfeld, Wunmi MosakuGenre: Horror/actionSummary: Twin brothers return to their hometown in Mississippi, only to confront a supernatural evil that forces them to fight for survival. Where to watch: HBO Max, Amazon Prime VideoREVIEW: When studios give directors creative opportunities to develop their own original stories and take them to the big screen, this is what we get: A fully immersive, politically and historically significant masterpiece that explores the innate experiences that make us human. Director Ryan Coogler brings artistic freedom that focuses heavily on necessary world-building, cultural elements and a nearly hypnotic environment that creates a next-level horror element. The distinctiveness in his use of light, fog and shadows cannot be understated. "Sinners" is wildly ambitious, but all of the pieces work together with such ease. 1. One Battle After AnotherDirector: Paul Thomas AndersonStarring: Leonardo DiCaprio, Sean Penn, Chase InfinitiGenre: Action thrillerSummary: A retired revolutionary living off the grid with his daughter is forced to fight back after a past enemy reappears years later.Where to watch: HBO MaxREVIEW: There is no way to express the greatness of "One Battle After Another" without sounding like a direct sponsor for the film. Put simply, it's an anxiety-inducing experience that feels equal to being hunted by enemies for hours on end. Profound tension is found at every doorstep, and fear follows behind in every sequence, breathing straight down your neck. This film is technically brilliant, radical and immersive, with a political message so worthwhile that it will carry forth for decades at the least. Even when your heart is racing and your palms are sweaty, "One Battle After Another" is Paul Thomas Anderson's masterful 162-minute rollercoaster that you never want to escape from. I truly believe "One Battle After Another" will be this year's Best Picture winner. Even if it doesn't win the actual award, this film is the real winner of 2025, and perhaps even this decade. Trust me, you don't want to miss this one.The 98th Academy Awards, hosted by Conan O'Brien, will take place starting at 7 p.m. on Sunday, March 15.
